newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO panel says EU breaks trade rules over bananas.
newsitem.headline: WTO panel says EU breaks trade rules over bananas.

text.p: A World Trade Organisation panel has upheld a complaint by the United States and four Latin American countries against the European Union's policy on banana imports, diplomats said Tuesday.
The WTO's dispute panel found the European Union's banana policy, which favours imports from mainly Caribbean countries, violated open trading rules, the diplomats said.

The diplomats said an interim report from the three-man panel in effect backed a complaint by the United States and Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico the EU discriminated against their marketing companies and producers.

The report, issued after nearly 10 months of deliberations, recommended that the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body ask the EU to bring the policy into line with its obligations under global trade accords, they added.

"As I see it, the report goes to the heart of the regime. I cannot see how the EU can avoid doing something about bringing its current practices into conformity with the agreements it has signed up to," said one trade envoy.

The finding -- which has to be confirmed in a final report to be issued publicly once comments have come in from all countries involved -- will come as a bitter blow to small Caribbean banana-producing nations, trade analysts said.

Those countries and the EU have argued that unless the preferences they enjoy for exports of the fruit to the European market are maintained, their economies will collapse under competition from the much larger-scale banana industry of Latin America.
The main Caribbean states involved are Jamaica, Belize, Surinam and the Windward Islands. Bananas are a key item in their foreign trade.

According to the diplomats, the panellists from Hong Kong, Switzerland and Australia found that the 1993 EU policy ran against several articles of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and against a related services accord.

Once the report has been finalised, the EU can ask the WTO appellate body for a review. But if that finding goes against it, under the tough WTO rules the EU will have to fall in with the recommendations or face WTO-approved sanctions.
Alternatively, it could maintain the policy but pay compensation to the United States and the four Latin American countries equal to the value of the trade they are losing because of it.
